ts-loja-fora-do-ar.enunciado:
We updated the store last night and the site hasn’t opened since. The intern already restarted everything twice, and nothing.

Jorge, who owns the ground-floor shop

Make curl http://loja.local (from your computer, through the Ingress entrance) respond. There’s more than one defect: each fix reveals the next.
ts-loja-fora-do-ar.dica: kubectl get pods; kubectl describe pod NAME (Events); kubectl get endpoints loja; kubectl describe svc loja. One defect at a time.
ts-loja-fora-do-ar.vidaReal: The store won’t open, and the problem could be in the merchandise (the image), in the clerk (the probe) or in the phone extension (the Service): the building manager checks them one by one, from the stockroom to the front desk.
ts-loja-fora-do-ar.limite: At a real store, you can see the counter is closed. In the cluster, each layer fails silently: only the events, the endpoints and describe tell you what’s going on.
ts-loja-fora-do-ar.comoSaber: curl http://loja.local returns the store’s JSON, with all 3 replicas ready.
ts-loja-fora-do-ar.relato: We updated the store last night and the site hasn’t opened since. The intern already restarted everything twice, and nothing.
ts-loja-fora-do-ar.morador: Jorge, who owns the ground-floor shop

ts-ninguem-se-acha.enunciado:
Since last night’s cleanup, nothing can find anything: the vitrine (storefront) can’t find the estoque (stockroom), and even the caretaker’s test pod says “bad address.” The cleanup crew swears they only turned off what wasn’t being used.

Célia, from the stockroom

Get the pods finding Services by name again: cliente (in default) and vitrine (in the loja namespace) need to call http://estoque.estoque. The store’s turnstile must keep blocking everything else.
ts-ninguem-se-acha.dica: When everything fails at once, look at what everyone uses: kubectl get deploy -n kube-system. Then, if vitrine still can’t find it: kubectl get networkpolicy -n loja.
ts-ninguem-se-acha.vidaReal: The condo’s switchboard operator (CoreDNS) was let go in the cleanup: nobody can get anybody’s number. And in the store’s block, the turnstile only lets people through to the stockroom, and forgot to let them call the switchboard operator.
ts-ninguem-se-acha.limite: Without the switchboard operator, anyone who knows the IP by heart can still call: DNS isn’t the network, it’s just the phone book.
ts-ninguem-se-acha.comoSaber: From both pods, wget -qO- http://estoque.estoque responds; from vitrine, http://admin.default stays blocked.
ts-ninguem-se-acha.relato:
Since last night’s cleanup, nothing can find anything: the vitrine (storefront) can’t find the estoque (stockroom), and even the caretaker’s test pod says
             “bad address.” The cleanup crew swears they only turned off what wasn’t being used.

ts-fila-parada.enunciado:
The monthly report hasn’t run since yesterday’s maintenance. The maintenance crew said they were done and left. Oh, and just to be safe, I increased the memory the report asks for.

Lima, from finance

Get both replicas of relatorio running. The node maintenance is over: put the nodes back in service (no working around it with tolerations).
ts-fila-parada.dica: kubectl describe pod NAME (the scheduler’s message changes with each fix); kubectl get nodes; kubectl describe node node-2 (Taints). To remove a taint: kubectl taint nodes NODE key=value:Effect- (with the hyphen at the end).
ts-fila-parada.vidaReal: The reports are waiting at the front gate: one building still has tape across its door, the other has the “under renovation” sign, and the request says each report needs a whole floor (300Gi) instead of a room (300Mi).
ts-fila-parada.limite: The doorman explains everything at once. The scheduler also lists the reason for each node, but a node blocked by the tape doesn’t even get measured: the next reason only shows up after the first fix.
ts-fila-parada.comoSaber: Both replicas of relatorio running, and no node closed off or with the maintenance sign.
ts-fila-parada.relato:
The monthly report hasn’t run since yesterday’s maintenance. The maintenance crew said they were done and left.
             Oh, and just to be safe, I increased the memory the report asks for.

msgs.2: node-2 no longer has the maintenance sign

ts-imagem-particular.titulo: The cash register that never arrives
ts-imagem-particular.enunciado:
We bought the new cash register software and IT installed it yesterday: they even put the registry login in a safe, they said. But the register won’t open, and the error says the image doesn’t even exist. It does: I can see it on Docker Hub, with our login!

Neide, from the bakery

Get both replicas of caixa (cash register, in the padaria namespace) running with the image kubelearn/caixa:1.0, which is private. There’s more than one defect: each fix reveals the next.
ts-imagem-particular.dica: kubectl describe pod -n padaria NAME (Events: “may require authorization”). The pod only uses the badge listed in imagePullSecrets. Then: kubectl get events -n padaria (FailedToRetrieveImagePullSecret) and kubectl get secrets -A: a Secret only counts in its own namespace.
ts-imagem-particular.vidaReal: The new register sits in the warehouse of a supplier that only delivers to whoever shows a badge. The badge was made, but nobody told the delivery person to bring it, and it ended up in the safe of another block.
ts-imagem-particular.limite: A real supplier would say “you don’t have access.” Docker Hub gives the same answer for an image that doesn’t exist and for a private image without a login, so it doesn’t tell strangers what it has.
ts-imagem-particular.relato:
We bought the new cash register software and IT installed it yesterday: they even put the registry login in a safe, they said.
             But the register won’t open, and the error says the image doesn’t even exist. It does: I can see it on Docker Hub, with our login!

ts-cardapio-de-ontem.enunciado:
Last night I changed the dish of the day on the bulletin board, like always: today it’s moqueca. But some customers see yesterday’s feijoada, and some see a page that says “It works!”. What is that?

Bento, from the ground-floor restaurant

Make the cardapio (menu) Service (in the restaurante namespace) always show today’s dish, which is in the cardapio ConfigMap. And make the next change on the board show up by itself, without restarting anything.
ts-cardapio-de-ontem.dica: kubectl get endpoints -n restaurante and kubectl get pods -n restaurante --show-labels: who else answers this extension? Then: kubectl get deploy cardapio -n restaurante -o yaml (volumeMounts). A file mounted with subPath never gets the new version of the ConfigMap.
ts-cardapio-de-ontem.vidaReal: Two clerks on the same phone extension: the old site’s, which nobody turned off, and the menu’s. And the menu clerk doesn’t read the bulletin board: they read a photocopy made the day they arrived.
ts-cardapio-de-ontem.limite: Without subPath, the kubelet swaps the mounted file by itself, but not right away (around a minute), and the program has to read the file again (nginx reads it on every request). An environment variable from a ConfigMap never changes: only in a new container.
ts-cardapio-de-ontem.comoSaber: From any pod, wget -qO- http://cardapio.restaurante always shows the moqueca, and the Deployment mounts the board without subPath.
ts-cardapio-de-ontem.relato:
Last night I changed the dish of the day on the bulletin board, like always: today it’s moqueca. But some customers see
             yesterday’s feijoada, and some see a page that says “It works!”. What is that?

msgs.0: only the menu answers the extension
msgs.2: the board is mounted without subPath (the next change shows up by itself)

ts-cracha-do-suporte.enunciado:
They gave me a badge to handle the store’s tickets, but it doesn’t open anything: not even the list of pods in the store’s block. And once it does, I need to read the logs and get into the cash register to investigate.

Bia, from support

Fix Bia’s badge (the user bia) in the loja namespace: she needs to list the pods, read the logs and get into them with kubectl exec. Without being able to delete anything. Test as her, with --as=bia.
ts-cracha-do-suporte.dica: kubectl get pods -n loja --as=bia and kubectl describe rolebinding suporte -n loja (the name under Subjects). Logs and exec are subresources: pods/log (get) and pods/exec (create). Check with kubectl auth can-i get pods --subresource=log -n loja --as=bia.
ts-cracha-do-suporte.vidaReal: The badge was printed with the name “Bia” and the turnstile looks for “bia”. And even with the right name, it only opened the apartments’ door: the incident book (logs) and the key to get in (exec) are separate doors.
ts-cracha-do-suporte.limite: At the front gate, someone would look at the badge and let Bia through. RBAC compares the name letter by letter, and doesn’t warn you that the binding points to a user who never shows up.
ts-cracha-do-suporte.comoSaber: With --as=bia: kubectl get pods -n loja, kubectl logs caixa -n loja and kubectl exec caixa -n loja -- ls work; kubectl delete pod caixa -n loja is refused.
ts-cracha-do-suporte.relato:
They gave me a badge to handle the store’s tickets, but it doesn’t open anything: not even the list of pods in the store’s
             block. And once it does, I need to read the logs and get into the cash register to investigate.

ts-normas-so-no-papel.titulo: The fire code on paper only
ts-normas-so-no-papel.enunciado:
At today’s inspection, the billing app in the pagamentos block was running as root, with every power there is. The restricted fire code sign is right there on the block’s door, but apparently it doesn’t stop anyone.

Captain Rocha, from the fire marshals

Make the pagamentos namespace block (not just warn about) pods that break the restricted standard, with both cobranca (billing) replicas running within it. Billing runs fine as any user other than root (1000, for example).
ts-normas-so-no-papel.dica: kubectl get ns pagamentos --show-labels: warn only warns, enforce blocks. Pods that are already running aren’t kicked out (at most, a warning): to see whether billing meets the standard, create new pods (kubectl rollout restart deployment/cobranca -n pagamentos) and look at kubectl describe rs -n pagamentos. Then, kubectl describe pod (runAsNonRoot).
ts-normas-so-no-papel.vidaReal: The fire marshals’ sign was hung in “warning” mode: the doorman read the code out loud and let people in anyway. Switching to “block” doesn’t evict whoever is already inside: it only applies to whoever arrives.
ts-normas-so-no-papel.limite: Passing the standard doesn’t make the program secure: it only ensures it starts without powers it doesn’t need.
ts-normas-so-no-papel.comoSaber: kubectl get pods -n pagamentos: 2 cobranca pods ready, created after the code took effect; and the namespace with pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted.
ts-normas-so-no-papel.relato:
At today’s inspection, the billing app in the pagamentos block was running as root, with every power there is. The restricted
             fire code sign is right there on the block’s door, but apparently it doesn’t stop anyone.
ts-normas-so-no-papel.morador: Captain Rocha, from the fire marshals

msgs.0: the block stops whoever breaks the code
msgs.3: all pods are from the version that meets the code

ts-promocao-que-nao-abre.titulo: The sale that closed the store
ts-promocao-que-nao-abre.enunciado:
I asked my nephew to turn on the store’s sale mode. While he was at it, he copied a “health check” from another site, which he said is what professionals do. The store hasn’t opened since.

Jorge, who owns the ground-floor shop

Get the loja (store) answering through the loja Service again, without restarting on its own, in sale mode (the /loja program takes --modo promocao) and keeping the livenessProbe: it’s a good idea, it just has to be right.
ts-promocao-que-nao-abre.dica: kubectl describe pod NAME (Last State: Terminated, Reason: StartError, exec: "--modo": executable file not found). The arguments go in args. Then: kubectl get pods (RESTARTS going up) and kubectl get events (Liveness probe failed: connection refused). Which port does the store listen on?
ts-promocao-que-nao-abre.vidaReal: The note said “open the store in sale mode,” and the nephew wrote just “sale mode” where the employee’s name goes: nobody was called in to open. And the health inspector knocks on the door of the room next door (80): since nobody answers there, he sends the employee home every half minute.
ts-promocao-que-nao-abre.limite: In a container, command replaces the program the image runs (the ENTRYPOINT); args only replaces its arguments. A wrong livenessProbe is worse than none: it restarts a program that was working.
ts-promocao-que-nao-abre.comoSaber: kubectl get pods: both replicas ready, with RESTARTS stuck at 0; and kubectl exec cliente -- wget -qO- http://loja responds.
ts-promocao-que-nao-abre.relato:
I asked my nephew to turn on the store’s sale mode. While he was at it, he copied a “health check” from another
             site, which he said is what professionals do. The store hasn’t opened since.
ts-promocao-que-nao-abre.morador: Jorge, who owns the ground-floor shop

msgs.2: the store is in sale mode

ts-relatorio-sem-folego.titulo: The report that runs out of breath
ts-relatorio-sem-folego.enunciado:
The report starts, crashes, starts again, crashes again. They said it’s out of memory, but I didn’t set any memory limit: look at the YAML! Oh, and management already approved up to 1Gi per container in finance.

Lima, from finance

Get both replicas of relatorio (report, in the financeiro namespace) running. The report loads the whole spreadsheet into memory (about 300Mi): declare its memory limit in the Deployment itself (512Mi gives some headroom). The block’s ceiling can go up to 1Gi, but it can’t disappear.
ts-relatorio-sem-folego.dica: kubectl describe pod -n financeiro NAME (Last State: OOMKilled; Limits; and the kubernetes.io/limit-ranger annotation). Who set the limit? kubectl describe limitrange -n financeiro. After declaring the limit: kubectl describe rs -n financeiro (FailedCreate).
ts-relatorio-sem-folego.vidaReal: The apartment’s blueprint came without a circuit breaker, so the management office installed the block’s standard breaker, too small for the accounting machine. And the block also has a ceiling: a breaker bigger than that isn’t even allowed in.
ts-relatorio-sem-folego.limite: A LimitRange only acts when the pod is created: changing the default or the ceiling doesn’t touch pods that already exist. That’s why the hidden limit shows up on the pod (kubectl describe pod), not in your YAML.
ts-relatorio-sem-folego.comoSaber: kubectl get pods -n financeiro: 2 relatorio pods Running, without restarting.
ts-relatorio-sem-folego.relato:
The report starts, crashes, starts again, crashes again. They said it’s out of memory, but I didn’t set any memory
             limit: look at the YAML! Oh, and management already approved up to 1Gi per container in finance.

msgs.1: the report declares its own memory limit
msgs.2: the block still has a ceiling
